raw_text:
Transcaval access is a fully percutaneous, transfemoral venous route for delivering large-bore devices into the abdominal aorta by intentionally creating a temporary aortocaval tract. The method arose from preclinical work showing that aortic bleeding can decompress into the adjacent inferior vena cava rather than the retroperitoneum [1]. Early human experience established feasibility in patients otherwise ineligible for transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) [2], and subsequent computed tomography (CT) planning work defined the anatomic requirements for a safe calcium-free aortic target, absence of interposed bowel, adequate distance from visceral branches, and a bailout covered-stent plan [3]. Practical technique descriptions then standardized electrosurgical wire traversal, snare capture, sheath delivery, and closure with nitinol occluders [4].

The principal structural heart application has been TAVR in patients with hostile iliofemoral arteries. Transcaval TAVR is attractive because it preserves transfemoral-like ergonomics, avoids thoracotomy, and can be performed without surgical cut-down. It has also proved adaptable in complex anatomy, including prior polyester aortic grafts [5], duplicated inferior vena cava [19], abdominal aortic grafts without a sheath [20], and even selected aneurysmal targets [21], [22]. The key physiologic concept is that retroperitoneal interstitial pressure exceeds caval pressure, favoring decompression of bleeding into the venous system; however, this protective mechanism depends on maintaining an open caval egress path until definitive closure.

Clinical evidence has progressed from case series to prospective and comparative studies. In the NHLBI prospective investigation, transcaval access and closure were successful in nearly all attempted patients, although bleeding, transfusion, and residual fistulae were important early safety signals [6]. Follow-up imaging from the same program showed that most residual aortocaval tracts closed over time, with very low late patency and no signal for delayed occluder migration or fracture [8]. The European multicenter registry confirmed feasibility across centers [9], and observational comparisons suggested outcomes broadly comparable with other nonfemoral approaches [10], [11]. A contemporary propensity-weighted comparison found transcaval TAVR associated with lower stroke than transaxillary access, with similar major bleeding, supporting its role as a nonthoracic alternative when iliofemoral arteries are unsuitable [12]. Recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses have reinforced that transcaval TAVR is feasible, with acceptable short-term mortality and vascular complication rates in anatomically selected, high-risk patients [14], [15].

Technique remains the determinant of safety. Preprocedural CT should identify a target where the cava and aorta are adjacent, the aortic wall is relatively free of calcium, the sheath will reach from the femoral vein, and a covered stent can be deployed if closure fails [3], [7]. Electrosurgical traversal is usually performed with a stiff 0.014-inch guidewire directed from the cava toward an aortic snare, followed by exchange for a rigid 0.035-inch rail and delivery of the TAVR sheath [4], [13]. Closure is commonly performed with a first-generation Amplatzer duct occluder, but the device is off-label and not purpose-built; first-in-human experience with a dedicated closure device suggests a pathway toward more predictable hemostasis [23]. Adjunctive strategies include protamine reversal, balloon tamponade, covered stent implantation, laser-assisted traversal through hostile calcium, and transradial secondary access to reduce femoral arterial instrumentation [16], [25].

The scope of transcaval access now extends beyond aortic valve replacement. Transcatheter electrosurgery has become a broader enabling platform for structural interventions that require intentional tissue traversal, including transcaval access and other procedures such as leaflet laceration [24]. Transcaval large-bore access has also been used for thoracic endovascular aortic repair in patients without adequate arterial access [26], for high-flow Impella support in cardiogenic shock or high-risk percutaneous intervention when arterial access would threaten limb ischemia [27], [28], and for modified left atrial venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation [29]. These applications are not “structural heart” in the narrow valve-repair sense, but they are directly relevant to structural programs because they share imaging, large-bore access, electrosurgical, and bailout skills [30].

Patient selection should be conservative during adoption. Ideal candidates have prohibitive transfemoral arterial anatomy but a favorable caval-aortic relationship, tolerable transient left-to-right shunting, correctable coagulopathy, and a realistic bailout plan. Severe right ventricular failure or pulmonary hypertension may make even a small acute aortocaval shunt poorly tolerated. Programs should maintain a standardized equipment checklist, rehearse covered-stent bailout, use experienced proctoring, and integrate interventional cardiology, structural imaging, anesthesia, and vascular surgery expertise. In contemporary practice, transcaval access is best viewed not as a rescue curiosity, but as a reproducible nonfemoral strategy for selected structural heart patients and a platform technology for other large-bore cardiovascular interventions.
